items.title: In Francia c’è lo sciopero generale, dopo tre sabati di proteste
items.summary: Era stato convocato prima delle manifestazioni, contro il carovita e la legge di bilancio: in mattinata i cortei sono stati per lo più pacifici
items.content:
Da giovedì mattina in Francia sono in corso manifestazioni in diverse città per uno sciopero generale convocato dai sindacati un mese fa. Finora i cortei sono stati in gran parte pacifici: gli scontri con la polizia si sono limitati ad alcuni gruppi di persone e non sono stati paragonabili a quelli molto più violenti che si erano visti sabato 17 ottobre . Le manifestazioni dei sabati successivi erano andate meglio, anche per l’eccezionale dispiegamento di polizia ordinato dal governo. Anche giovedì sono stati schierati 70mila agenti su tutto il territorio francese, come in occasione delle ultime grandi proteste.

Secondo le stime preliminari del ministero dell’Interno i manifestanti sono stati 600mila in tutta la Francia. Oltre alle molte manifestazioni dei sindacati ci sono state mobilitazioni organizzate autonomamente su Telegram e Signal , con altre decine di cortei non ufficiali e proteste davanti a centinaia di licei e università. Ci sono disagi al trasporto aereo e ferroviario, negli ospedali, nelle scuole e in altri servizi pubblici, ed è rimasta chiusa anche la Tour Eiffel. Il ministero dell’Istruzione ha stimato che il 16 per cento degli insegnanti ha scioperato.

L’ultima manifestazione a concludersi è stata quella di Parigi (nelle altre città sono iniziate e finite in mattinata). Qui il corteo era partito alle 14 da Place de la République, ma poco dopo si era bloccato perché la polizia aveva fatto delle cariche contro un gruppo di manifestanti violenti, a circa due chilometri di distanza. La manifestazione è rimasta in gran parte pacifica, ma a un certo punto in Place de la République si era creata una grande folla, che non era riuscita a defluire perché il percorso della manifestazione era fermo a causa degli scontri. Il corteo è finito in Place de la Nation: per lasciare la piazza bisognava fare la fila e attraversare un cordone di polizia che controllava rapidamente gli zaini.

Studenti di fronte all’università di Lione (AP Photo/Laurent Cipriani)

Prima della partenza del corteo principale c’erano state alcune manifestazioni non autorizzate. A metà mattina un gruppo di liceali aveva provato a bloccare la centrale Rue de Rivoli, ma era stato rapidamente sgomberato dalla polizia.

In mattinata ci sono stati cortei in molte città, incluso sull’isola della Réunion, un territorio francese nell’oceano Indiano. Fra i più grandi ci sono stati quelli a Lione e a Marsiglia, dove si stima abbiano partecipato decine di migliaia di persone. Sono stati per lo più tranquilli e pacifici, spesso con un’atmosfera festosa, anche se c’è stato qualche momento di tensione con la polizia. In alcuni casi gli scontri peggiori e gli atti di vandalismo sono avvenuti dopo la fine dei cortei organizzati, da parte di piccoli gruppi.

A Lione ci sono stati scontri fra gli agenti e un gruppo isolato di manifestanti (i media francesi li hanno descritti come “black bloc”). A Rennes nel pomeriggio i rappresentanti dei sindacati sono stati attaccati da persone a volto coperto, in una situazione confusa a cui la polizia ha risposto con una carica e arrestando sia i sindacalisti che gli aggressori.

Ci sono state anche proteste e picchetti in decine di licei, a volte con barricate improvvisate e cassonetti dati alle fiamme, e in alcuni casi la polizia è intervenuta per sgomberarli. Il governo aveva detto a metà mattina che gli istituti interessati erano 81 (sui 3.700 in tutta la Francia). In un liceo di Tournefeuille, alla periferia di Tolosa (nel sud-ovest della Francia), c’è stato un incendio, dopo che delle persone ci avevano acceso dentro dei petardi. In altre città ci sono stati scontri violenti fra polizia e liceali, e in mattinata a Rennes gli agenti sono stati colpiti da lanci di bocce per il gioco della pétanque .

Manifestanti a Lione, il 5 novembre (AP Photo/Laurent Cipriani)

Lo sciopero e le manifestazioni erano state indette dai sindacati principalmente per chiedere di aumentare il salario minimo e di potenziare i programmi sociali, e per contestare la legge di bilancio presentata dal governo. Nella sua forma attuale è «catastrofica per il paese», secondo Sophie Binet, la segretaria generale della CGT, uno dei principali sindacati. Dopo le manifestazioni il primo ministro Sébastien Lecornu ha indetto una riunione fra i sindacati e i rappresentanti delle aziende per «trovare risposte alle domande sul potere d’acquisto e sui salari».

Ci si aspetta che a giorni la legge di bilancio venga bocciata dal parlamento, dove è stata seppellita di emendamenti dai vari partiti. Lecornu è espresso dallo schieramento centrista del presidente Emmanuel Macron, che non ha una maggioranza stabile, e le proteste sono diventate motivo di accuse incrociate tra i partiti.

Nelle scorse settimane, dopo un incontro coi sindacati, Lecornu aveva prospettato la possibilità di anticipare l’aggiornamento del salario minimo, che di solito avviene a inizio gennaio. Il suo governo aveva anche già fatto concessioni agli studenti : una graduale sostituzione del criticato sistema di accesso all’università (il Parcoursup ), un limite alle dimensioni delle classi e un fondo per le ristrutturazioni degli edifici.

Sulla legge di bilancio probabilmente c’è meno margine. Da anni i governi francesi devono misurarsi con la necessità di contenere il debito pubblico e limitare la spesa, senza maggioranze definite in parlamento: per disaccordi sulla legge di bilancio erano caduti entrambi i predecessori di Lecornu, François Bayrou e Michel Barnier , e lui stesso un anno fa si era dimesso, prima di venire rimesso al suo posto da Macron.

Il governo è stato contestato per la risposta muscolare alle manifestazioni. Dopo aver ammesso di avere « perso il controllo » di quelle del 17 ottobre, aveva introdotto alcuni giorni di coprifuoco nelle città e Macron aveva ordinato ai prefetti di limitare il più possibile le manifestazioni.

items.title: Il governo indonesiano sta mobilitando migliaia di soldati a Giacarta, dopo uno scandalo sulle intercettazioni del presidente
items.content:
L’esercito indonesiano ha inviato migliaia di militari a Giacarta, la capitale del paese, dopo l’arresto di tre importanti funzionari di polizia accusati di aver intercettato illegalmente le comunicazioni del presidente Prabowo Subianto e di altri politici. Inizialmente si era parlato di un grosso dispiegamento, di quasi 21mila soldati: finora in città ne sono arrivati circa 7mila. L’esercito ha detto che i soldati serviranno a mantenere «la sicurezza nazionale» e per alcune esercitazioni: non è stato chiarito se l’invio dei soldati abbia qualche legame con lo scandalo delle intercettazioni.

Prabowo guida il partito nazionalista di destra Gerindra e in passato è stato accusato di violazioni dei diritti umani e di voler estendere il ruolo dell’esercito alla vita pubblica per rafforzare il proprio potere. Oltre allo scandalo delle intercettazioni, che secondo alcuni dirigenti del suo governo sta mettendo a rischio la stabilità del suo governo, nei giorni scorsi c’erano state grosse proteste organizzate da studenti contro di lui. La sua popolarità è in forte calo: secondo un sondaggio pubblicato a ottobre, il consenso nei suoi confronti in un anno è passato dall’81,2 al 44,5 per cento.

items.title: Il calore che rigenera: guida alle terme più spettacolari per una “fuga d’inverno”
items.summary: Niente nella stagione fredda rilassa come un passaggi nei paradisi termali. Dalla Valle d'Aosta alla Toscana, con uno sguardo alle vicinissime Carinzia e Croazia, otto mete imperdibili tra storia, natura e relax
items.content:
L’inverno è la stagione delle contraddizioni, una finestra temporale che avvolge il tam tam lavorativo di ogni giorno con temperature rigide e colori algidi, rispondendo alla frenesia col silenzio di mattinate gelide e buie, e al caos con l’immobilismo di una natura che ci guarda spoglia e muta. La fuga ideale in cerca di relax sono le classiche terme, ambienti usati fin dall’antichità per restituire al corpo il beneficio del calore che attiva la microcircolazione e stimola le difese immunitarie, oggi veri e propri microcosmi dedicati al benessere, dove tra un messaggio e una sauna l’organismo ritrova l’equilibrio, o almeno si concede una pausa. L’Italia è uno dei Paesi europei dove gli stabilimenti termali sono non solo ben attrezzati ma anche spettacolari da vedere e da vivere. Ecco una carrellata di quelli imperdibili, con uno sguardo all’estero.

A Pré-Saint-Didier , caratteristico comune di circa 940 abitanti nella Valdigne in Valle d'Aosta , ai piedi del Monte Bianco , ci si può rilassare all'aperto circondati dalla neve: il giardino, infatti, offre tre piscine esterne e saune ricavate in baite di legno, con vetrate panoramiche sulla catena del Monte Bianco. Il percorso benessere comprende vasche idromassaggio, vasche relax con musica subacquea, cascate tonificanti e servizi termali innovativi, saune a tema in chalet di legno, bagni di vapore aromatizzati, area fanghi, sale di cromoterapia e di aromaterapia, sale relax panoramiche. Esperti terapisti praticano massaggi rilassanti e tonificanti. Durante la giornata, il Maestro del benessere propone agli ospiti tecniche di rilassamento, esercizi e trattamenti per il corpo, maschere di bellezza e peeling aromatizzati. Per l'accesso alla spa è necessaria la prenotazione che si può effettuare online. Non è consentito l’ingresso ai minori di 14 anni. Le sorgenti naturali di Pré-Saint-Didier sgorgano in una grotta alla base della cascata dell’ Orrido , nei pressi dello stabilimento della spa. Le fonti della zona erano conosciute già in epoca romana, ma l'uso sistematico delle acque cominciò a metà del ’600, quando i primi forestieri venivano qui per “passare le acque”. Lo stabilimento risale al 1834 e l’edificio che ospitava il Casinò al 1888. Per oltre 150 anni le terme furono uno dei principali centri di attrazione della Valle d’Aosta, ospitarono personaggi illustri e divennero il luogo di villeggiatura preferito dalla famiglia reale italiana. Completamente restaurato dopo oltre 30 anni di chiusura, l'edificio è tornato al suo antico splendore, conservando l’architettura dell’epoca.

Sauna al pino mugo, alle erbe, con cromoterapia, finlandese e a infrarossi. Bagno turco, idromassaggio all'aperto, percorso Kneipp e zone relax. E, quando suona la campana, significa che l'Aufguss o il bagno di suoni stanno per cominciare. Esiste un luogo ad Andalo , in Trentino-Alto Adige , dove il tempo rallenta e il respiro si sintonizza con il ritmo della montagna. È il centro Acquain, il wellness di Andalo Life, day spa aperta a tutti e dedicata alla cultura della sauna nordica olistica, ovvero nata per essere un rifugio. Qui, tra le Dolomiti di Brenta e il Parco Naturale Adamello Brenta , le tradizioni del nord incontrano le radici del benessere più profondo, creando un’esperienza dove le ansie restano fuori dalla porta. Niente grandi vasche termali, ma un percorso di diverse saune, con diverse temperature e gradi di umidità, pensato per chi cerca il distacco dalla frenesia quotidiana attraverso il calore e il silenzio. All’interno del centro benessere non è ammesso il costume, ma è obbligatorio l’uso di un telo o di un accappatoio. Occorre prenotare online per garantirsi l’entrata.

Conclusa con successo la stagione estiva, che tra il 15 maggio e il 15 settembre 2026 ha fatto registrare oltre 167mila visitatori, le Terme Merano , in Trentino Alto-Adige , accolgono ora gli ospiti negli ambienti caldi e accoglienti dell'area sauna, fra trattamenti all’insegna del calore più profondo, massaggi con pietre di lava calde e bagni altoatesini al fieno di montagna, utili in caso di reumatismi e artrosi perché favoriscono la vascolarizzazione. Benefici anche i massaggi con olio aromatico, che intiepidito potenzia l'effetto distensivo sui muscoli e fa sprigionare al meglio le essenze delle erbe aromatiche. I massaggi al profumo di loto, frangipane o gelsomino aiutano invece a liberare la mente. Tanti anche i rituali pensati per due, dal Bagno di Sissi agli aromi altoatesini purificanti nella vasca imperiale all’idromassaggio alla stella alpina, all’uva o al sale, senza dimenticare la cabina infrarossi, che rilassa e scioglie le contratture e lenisce i dolori. La sauna al fieno biologico dell’Alto Adige propone una temperatura fra i 45 e i 60°C e prende ispirazione dal tradizionale maso tirolese. 45°C anche per il bagno di vapore al miele altoatesino, che riproduce appunto l’alveare delle api, mentre nel bagno di vapore Passerstein si può osservare l'acqua che scorre nel fiume Passirio , per un effetto rigenerante. Temperature molto più elevate nella sauna finlandese esterna, che raggiunge i 100°C e offre un ricco programma di Aufguss, tra gettate di vapore con maestro di sauna. Dopo la sauna, gli angoli attrezzati con divanetti e cuscini davanti al fuoco scoppiettante sono il posto ideale per chiudere la giornata.

Il Parco Termale del Garda di Villa dei Cedri è una splendida "SPA naturale" di 13 ettari situata a Colà di Lazise , a pochi minuti dalle rive del Lago di Garda . A differenza dei classici centri termali al chiuso, la struttura si sviluppa all'aperto, all'interno di un parco secolare ricco di cedri maestosi e piante rare, dove si trovano due grandi laghi termali originati da falde sotterranee profonde fino a 200 metri. Il giardino d’inverno si trova in prossimità del lago termale principale, dove si trovano gli spogliatoi (uomo e donna dotati di cabine, spazi comuni, docce, toilettes e asciuga capelli), armadietti disponibili fino ad esaurimento e cassettine di sicurezza porta valori gratuite. Il percorso saune comprende due saune finlandesi, una biosauna, un grande bagno turco con cromo e aromaterapia e una grande biosauna situata all’esterno nel giardino riservato al centro benessere. Il centro benessere è accessibile sia dalla clientela interna che esterna con ingresso diretto da Piazza di Sopra n. 4 Colà di Lazise ed è stato realizzato all’interno delle antiche scuderie per i cavalli di fine ‘800, trasformate in chiave moderna pur mantenendo le tracce dell’architettura del passato. Al piano superiore c’è la zona relax, una confortevole area riscaldata con un suggestivo camino. Nella stagione invernale sono anche disponibili dei lettini con vista sul lago termale.

C’è solo una cosa più rilassante di un weekend in un resort termale: un weekend in tre resort termali. In Toscana è possibile sperimentare la Wellness Tuscan Route, nuovo itinerario che unisce per la prima volta in un unico percorso i tre iconici resort termali toscani Fonteverde, Grotta Giusti e Bagni di Pisa. Un viaggio di sei notti, con soggiorni di due notti in ciascuna struttura, pensato per accompagnare gli ospiti alla scoperta di tre diverse interpretazioni del benessere. Alla base dell'esperienza c'è Equilibrium, filosofia che integra medicina preventiva, nutrizione, movimento, gestione dello stress e benefici delle acque termali in un approccio personalizzato. Fonteverde, nel cuore della Val d'Orcia (una parte della Toscana riconosciuta Patrimonio Unesco nel 2004), invita gli ospiti a rallentare attraverso le discipline orientali e la tradizione ayurvedica, accompagnati dal Maestro Dipu in percorsi finalizzati al riequilibrio delle energie fisiche e mentali, tra consulenze individuali, alimentazione ayurvedica, trattamenti corpo e massaggi. Punti forti di Grotta Giusti, storica villa ottocentesca immersa nella campagna toscana, celebre per custodire la più grande grotta termale naturale d'Europa, sono appunto il microclima della grotta, il lago termale sotterraneo e le proprietà terapeutiche delle acque. Il programma include anche sessioni di Pil-Oga e l'esclusiva esperienza di Spa Floating, pratica meditativa che si svolge nelle acque del lago sotterraneo. Bagni di Pisa punta invece sulla nutrizione e sul ruolo centrale del microbiota nel mantenimento della salute. Nello storico palazzo termale che fu residenza estiva del Granduca di Toscana, gli ospiti intraprendono un percorso guidato da un medico tutor, dietista e chef per approfondire i principi di un'alimentazione ispirata alla dieta mediterranea.

Ancora in Val d’Orcia in Toscana , ma in prossimità dello storico borgo medievale di Bagno Vignoni , noto per le sue rinomate acque termali, l’Adler Thermae è un santuario di benessere dove natura, eleganza e quiete trovano un equilibrio perfetto. Tra acque termali millenarie, paesaggi modellati dal tempo e ambienti che coniugano comfort contemporaneo e tradizione toscana, la vacanza diventa un percorso sensoriale di autentica rigenerazione. Vero gioiello del resort sono le acque: ipertermali e solfato-alcalino-terrose, sgorgano a pochi passi dal resort a circa 50°C e poi sono portate a 36°C nelle piscine aperte tutto l’anno, da quella termale interna ed esterna, particolarmente benefica per ossa, pelle e articolazioni, a quella per il nuoto. E, per chi desidera un’esperienza esclusiva, c’è la grotta salina con acqua termale a 38° arricchita con sali del Mar Morto, che purifica la pelle e stimola la circolazione. Il calore favorisce la respirazione, stimola la diuresi, scioglie le tensioni muscolari e migliora l’ossigenazione dei tessuti. Grazie ai minerali disciolti, queste acque sono particolarmente indicate per sostenere la salute dell’apparato osseo-articolare e della pelle, oltre che per alleviare disturbi come osteoartrosi, reumatismi extra-articolari, tendiniti, cellulite, alterazioni del circolo venoso e diverse affezioni ginecologiche e dermatologiche. Queste proprietà benefiche erano apprezzate anche nei secoli passati, tanto da conquistare personaggi illustri come Lorenzo il Magnifico e Santa Caterina da Siena, solo per citarne alcuni.

items.title: Il vice primo ministro della Baviera Hubert Aiwanger è stato trovato morto in una camera d’albergo di Berlino
items.content: Mercoledì il vice primo ministro della Baviera Hubert Aiwanger è stato trovato morto in una camera dell’hotel Neuer Fritz di Berlino: aveva 55 anni ed era anche ministro statale dell’Economia e leader del partito di centrodestra Freie Wähler (Liberi Elettori). Non si conoscono ancora le cause della morte: la procura di Berlino e la polizia hanno avviato un’indagine. Secondo il Tagesspiegel , le autorità ritengono che sia morto per cause naturali. Il quotidiano Bild scrive che poche ore prima si era sentito male e aveva cancellato l’impegno per cui si trovava a Berlino: un discorso per l’apertura della sede cittadina del suo partito.

items.title: La condanna del noto attivista pro-democrazia di Hong Kong Joshua Wong
items.summary: A dieci anni di carcere, per aver cospirato per convincere paesi stranieri a imporre sanzioni contro la Cina e il governo della città
items.content:
Joshua Wong, uno dei principali esponenti del movimento per la democrazia di Hong Kong, è stato condannato a dieci anni di carcere per aver cospirato con altri attivisti per convincere governi stranieri a imporre sanzioni contro la Cina e Hong Kong.

Wong, che ha 30 anni, era diventato famoso quando era ancora adolescente, guidando le proteste contro i tentativi del governo di Hong Kong di introdurre nelle scuole un programma di educazione patriottica. Nel 2014 fu uno dei leader delle manifestazioni studentesche pro-democrazia diventate note come “movimento degli ombrelli” , e poi partecipò alle grandi proteste antigovernative dell’estate del 2019.

Wong si era dichiarato colpevole a settembre. Secondo il giudice, lui e l’attivista Nathan Law, che vive in esilio nel Regno Unito, erano i principali responsabili di una campagna per sollecitare governi stranieri ad adottare sanzioni e altre misure contro la Cina e Hong Kong.

Hong Kong è una città formalmente autonoma che fa parte della Cina e che per decenni aveva goduto di un ampio grado di libertà e indipendenza rispetto al resto del paese. A partire dalla repressione delle proteste del 2019 quest’autonomia è stata progressivamente eliminata: la Cina ha perseguitato sistematicamente i sostenitori del movimento pro-democrazia e ha annullato buona parte dei diritti in precedenza garantiti alla città, soprattutto con l’introduzione della severissima legge sulla sicurezza nazionale , che ha limitato moltissimo la possibilità di criticare il regime cinese.

Wong era già in carcere da quasi sei anni per un’altra condanna . In quel caso Wong aveva confessato di aver organizzato una protesta fuori dalla sede della polizia. Avrebbe dovuto finire di scontare la pena a gennaio del 2027.

items.title: Salvini embraces Musk’s self-driving vision. But Italian law stands in the way
items.summary: The transport minister wants swift approval of Tesla’s driving system, but vehicle certification, liability issues and restrictions on road use mean there is still a long way to go before driverless cars become a reality
items.content:
ROME – A “very positive and constructive” conversation. That was how Italy’s Minister of Infrastructure and Transport, Matteo Salvini , described his call with Elon Musk , the owner of Tesla, to discuss autonomous driving.

Autonomous driving remains a marginal reality in Italy and across Europe, if not virtually non-existent. And the conversation between the two has reignited the debate.

Salvini himself reported the exchange on X, confirming the Italian government's interest in new technologies and expressing hope that Europe would swiftly approve the advanced driver-assistance system developed by Tesla.

Very positive and constructive conversation with @elonmusk today. Italy is looking with great interest at the opportunities offered by assisted driving technologies, with a focus on innovation and road safety, and supports a swift EU approval of Tesla Assisted Driving. Thanks for the exchange, Elon!

Speaking later at a logistics conference in Genoa focused on north-western Italy, the deputy prime minister said he had asked ministry officials “to open up, as far as current regulations allow, to innovations already being used in other countries”.

The aim is also to attract investment in technology and the automotive sectors. Of course, questions surrounding insurance and civil and criminal liability remain unresolved. But Salvini argues that these issues should not “close the door to the future”.

Despite its name, Tesla's Full Self-Driving (Supervised) system does not allow a car to drive entirely on its own. It can control steering, speed, lane changes and other manoeuvres, but the person behind the wheel must constantly monitor the road and be ready to intervene.

It is therefore an advanced driver-assistance system generally classified as Level 2 automation, meaning responsibility remains with the driver.

Levels 3 and 4, by contrast, allow vehicles to take over driving under certain conditions or within designated areas. This is the category that includes robotaxis, driverless shuttles and automated vehicles used in logistics.

Tesla is seeking approval through European vehicle type-approval procedures. Technical authorisation could make it easier for the company to enter the EU market, but it would not eliminate differences between national laws.

Brussels is primarily responsible for setting technical and safety requirements, while individual member states retain control over road use, insurance, access to public roads and liability in the event of an accident.

In Italy, on-road testing has been permitted since the 2018 Smart Road decree, but it requires ministerial authorisation, designated routes, insurance cover and a supervisor capable of intervening.

What is still missing, however, is a comprehensive regulatory framework allowing fully driverless vehicles to be deployed commercially.

One of the most sensitive issues concerns the supervisor. Requiring someone to be physically present on board could make services such as robotaxis and autonomous shuttles economically unviable.

Under Italy's current Highway Code, driverless vehicles are still not allowed to circulate freely on public roads.

Germany and France have already authorised automated driving in specific areas or along designated routes, subject to strict conditions and supervision. But Europe has yet to introduce any general liberalisation of driverless transport.

As of October 2026, robotaxis regularly carry passengers in 32 cities worldwide. In 17 of those cities, paid services operate without a driver on board, mainly in the United States and China. Not one of these cities is in Europe.

Regulators are also adapting their rules to accommodate vehicles without conventional steering wheels or pedals.

Waymo continues to expand its services, while an agreement with Toyota provides for trials in Japan from 2027 using electric SUVs equipped with Level 4 autonomous driving technology.

Trials and projects are also multiplying across Europe, from Copenhagen to Madrid, Zurich and London, involving companies such as Pony.ai, Uber and Vright, as well as operators including Baidu and Waymo. Yet the regulatory landscape remains fragmented.

In Italy, attention is also turning to Milan, where projects have been announced involving autonomous Fiat 500e cars developed with the start-up Niulinx, alongside automated car-sharing solutions from Neon Lynx, a company founded within the Polytechnic University of Milan.

The challenge now is to turn these trials into real-world services, striking a balance between innovation, safety and legal responsibility.

items.title: The ancient world in a gaze: Rome unveils the Fayum portraits
items.summary: From 5 November, Rome’s Ara Pacis Museum will showcase extraordinary Egyptian portraits from the second and third centuries AD, influenced by Greek and Roman artistic traditions
items.content:
ROME – The mystery that remains unsolved, ultimately, is why, after two thousand years, these portraits can still look us in the eye. How they can seem every bit as alive as the people standing before them.

There is no answer in the dimly lit galleries of the Ara Pacis, where The Power of Portraiture: Egypt and Rome. The Faces of Fayum opens to the public on 5 November (curated by Claudio Parisi Presicce and Laura Petacco, running until 2 May 2027, with a catalogue published by Allemandi).

Around 50 paintings have arrived from Cairo, the Louvre, the Getty in Los Angeles and the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. For the first time, they are being displayed alongside imperial sculptures from the same period. Only about a thousand examples of these portraits survive worldwide.

These are unique works, created between the first and third centuries AD and preserved thanks to their original purpose: they covered the faces of the dead, tucked among the bandages of their mummies.

In the Fayum oasis and elsewhere, in an Egypt now under Roman rule but still a crossroads of cultures and deeply influenced by Greek civilisation, these secular icons were being created centuries before the concept of the icon as we know it.

Against neutral backgrounds, there are no gods or goddesses, but recognisable men and women, with bright, expressive eyes, carefully arranged hairstyles and beards. Most are still young.

All appear to have been painted from life, with a realism that art history would not rediscover for centuries.

There is the portrait from Eton, with its stern, almost Pasolini-like expression. Or the Getty's Isidora, whose eyes seem fixed on something far away.

“We don't have all the answers to these mysteries,” says Parisi Presicce, Rome's Superintendent of Cultural Heritage. “Were they painted before or after the subjects died? On one example, we found a small cord. Does that mean the paintings were previously hung in people's homes?

“What we do know is that these masterpieces survived in Egypt because of the climate. But portrait painting of this quality was widespread throughout the eastern Mediterranean, as Pliny tells us.”

Another closely guarded secret lies within the Tondo of the Two Brothers , brought here from the Cairo Museum following a restoration carried out by Italian specialists.

While traditional Fayum portraits were painted in tempera or encaustic, using heated wax, on rectangular wooden panels, the circular shape and dimensions of this work suggest that it served a different purpose.

“What is significant is that the tondo consists of two wooden panels joined along the line dividing the two figures,” explains co-curator Laura Petacco.

“This construction would have made it possible to separate the two portraits and turn them into independent images. The fact that the tondo has survived in its original form suggests the importance attached to preserving the composition as a whole.

The value of the image therefore seems to lie not only in the possibility of identifying two individuals, but also in the representation of the relationship between them.”

The figure on the left, wearing a short red cloak and a white tunic decorated with a swastika — here an ancient solar symbol — is the younger of the two.

“Were they brothers? Father and son? Teacher and pupil? Or lovers?” asks Parisi Presicce. “What is certain, though, is that this is the most important work of antiquity.”

Its place of origin may offer a clue: Antinopolis, the city founded by Emperor Hadrian in memory of his beloved Antinous, who drowned in the Nile.

Paola Davoli, director of the Soknopaiou Nesos Project and professor of Egyptology at the University of Salento, is presenting for the first time one of the objects loaned by Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities: a painted wooden door panel depicting a boy, discovered at Dime es-Seba.

“This is not a funerary portrait,” the scholar explains, “but the image of a very young boy undergoing the ritual cutting of his sidelock, which marked his passage into adulthood.”

Egypt's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, Sherif Fathi Attia, speaks of peace and coexistence between cultures, and of a diplomatic bridge built through art between Italy and Egypt over the past seventy years.

He mentions Italian President Sergio Mattarella and the exhibition of treasures from the age of the pharaohs held at the Scuderie del Quirinale until last June.

“The faces of Fayum,” he concludes, “tell us a story of coexistence between Greeks, Romans and Egyptians. Not a clash, but a dialogue between civilisations that can still take place today.”

“It was in the Fayum portraits that I found the answer. There is no decoration there, no anecdote. There is only the gaze,” Henri Matisse once said.

Perhaps the soul of the world lies hidden in these portraits. That is why we recognise ourselves when we look at them.

They are our brothers and sisters, projected into an imagined world beyond our own, a place they seem to envision without war or torture.

items.title: Bottega Veneta’s Instagram comeback and the true value of luxury Social archives
items.summary: The Italian fashion house reactivates its account after five years of silence, finding 2.4 million followers still there and its grid untouched. The move reopens the debate on digital storefronts and the industry habit of wiping feeds with every creative turnover—only to restore them seasons later.
items.content:
In the canals of Venice, Italy’s most familiar greeting began as an act of devotion. “S’ciao,” people would say, bowing their heads before someone of standing—a shortened version of schiavo vostro , meaning "at your service."

With this ancient and ceremonious word, typeset in a serif font that evokes old Italian storefronts and 1960s editorial design, Bottega Veneta has chosen to switch its Instagram profile back on after more than five years of silence.

Waiting for the maison, founded in Vicenza in 1966, were 2.4 million followers—a mere 100,000 fewer than on 5 January 2021, the day then-creative director Daniel Lee wiped all of the brand's social accounts clean. It was like walking into a salon closed for the season, only to find the dust sheets still on the sofas and the guests seated in their exact places, composed and waiting for the hosts.

The return comes a year after the debut of Louise Trotter—who stepped in to carry on Matthieu Blazy’s legacy—and less than two months after the new CEO Romain Spitzer took office, as Kering seeks fresh momentum after several challenging seasons.

This seemingly minor piece of news sparks a much broader reflection on the purpose of luxury social media profiles—public archives that companies rush to empty with every creative handover, as if recent memory were an awkward guest that needed to be politely shown the door.

In December 1978, a double-page ad campaign conceived alongside Andy Warhol established the motto that still defines the house: "When your own initials are enough." The irony of history is that this manifesto of discretion was born alongside the prophet of fifteen minutes of fame, and that over forty years later, Daniel Lee took that principle to its logical extreme, extending the restraint from the logo to the very voice of the brand.

"Social media represents the homogenization of culture; everyone sees the exact same stream of content," the designer explained at the time. The account was replaced by Issued by Bottega , a quarterly digital journal, while François-Henri Pinault announced that the brand would rely much more heavily into its ambassadors and fans.

Those fans responded with an almost monastic devotion. The @newbottega page, run by brand enthusiasts, already boasted 350,000 followers by the time the official account went dark, and by 2023 the hashtag #NewBottega had surpassed 120,000 posts on Instagram and 22 million views on TikTok. In his famous chapter on secrecy from his 1908 work Sociology, sociologist Georg Simmel observed that what is hidden exerts an attraction independent of its actual content, granting whoever holds it an exceptional position. Bottega Veneta turned that intuition into strategy, and the financial results proved the brand right.

Revenues grew by 25 percent in 2021, the first year spent entirely away from social media; they surpassed 1.5 billion euros and rose to 1.7 billion in 2024 under Blazy, who honoured the vow of silence—indulging in only a brief stint on the Chinese platform Weibo—before moving to Chanel.

Yet the lesson of this long eclipse is more subtle than the financial reports suggest. In the luxury sector, desire is born primarily from the images that celebrities and fans pass from phone to phone, and the official channel is merely one voice—however authoritative—in a much larger chorus.

At the same time, prolonged withdrawal became a recognizable signature in its own right—a sort of monogram of absence. For a brand that had abandoned the logo, the risk of turning discretion into a formula was becoming very real.

Reopening the digital storefront today means admitting that even silence, like any style, has its seasons. It acknowledges that a new creative director needs a room where they can be heard, while a luxury market that has slowed down across multiple regions is searching for a direct dialogue with a younger audience. For a fashion house that once declared its independence from algorithms, returning to the stage with a word that originally meant "at your service" feels like a surrender signed with a fountain pen, full of grace and self-irony.

The blank grid with which Bottega Veneta re-emerges pushes a deeply entrenched industry habit to its limit. With every change of creative director, fashion houses empty their pages with the efficiency of an eviction, wiping years of runway shows and campaigns out overnight.

In April 2016, Saint Laurent deleted its entire Hedi Slimane-era archive—during which sales had nearly tripled—to publish a single portrait of Anthony Vaccarello. Two years later, upon arriving at Celine, Slimane dropped the accent from the brand's name and purged its account in one stroke, bidding farewell to the Phoebe Philo era. Daniel Lee repeated the gesture at Burberry in February 2023, just two weeks before his first runway show, earning a reputation as the fastest eraser in international fashion.

Gucci went a step further, wiping thousands of posts in September 2023 to welcome Sabato De Sarno, only to archive every image all over again just two years later when Catherine Opie’s portraits introduced Demna’s debut collection to its 52 million followers. Balenciaga emptied its feed in 2021, only to restore the old photographs in March 2023—in a back-and-forth worthy of Penelope’s web, woven by day and unravelled by night to keep suitors at bay.

Historians call damnatio memoriae the ancient Roman decree that erased the memory of disgraced emperors. In the Severan Tondo , a wooden family portrait from around 200 AD now housed in Berlin, the face of the young Geta was scraped away after his brother Caracalla had him assassinated.

Luxury brands repeat that gesture with infinitely more polite methods and a thoroughly contemporary paradox. Maisons invest substantial sums in archives and foundations to celebrate their distant past, while treating their recent past as a shadowy area to be cleared away in a hurry—almost as if history only gains dignity after a few decades of aging in a cellar.

Yet those profiles, originally born as simple shop windows, have become the most-consulted public archives for every fashion house—the places where a design student or a collector can trace recent history with a swipe of a thumb. Emptying them means sacrificing that function to the theatre of rebirth, turning every debut into a Year Zero and every designer into a founding father.

Instead, preservation is left to the fans—such as @oldceline, launched in September 2018 in the wake of Slimane’s purge and quickly transformed into a sanctuary for Philo-era nostalgics. It is much like Archimedes’ Palimpsest, a 10th-century manuscript scraped clean by a 13th-century monk to write a prayer book over it, where the Greek mathematician's lost treatises were eventually recovered thanks to multispectral imaging.

With creative tenures growing shorter and shorter—De Sarno lasted barely two years at Gucci—the canvas risks being unravelled faster than it can be woven. By starting over from a blank page, Bottega Veneta has pulled off the most radical gesture of all, granting Louise Trotter the freedom to tell her story right from line one.

After all, in Italian, “ciao” serves just as well for greeting as it does for parting. True to its proverbial reserve, the maison has carefully avoided clarifying which of the two meanings it had in mind. Followers are left with the pleasure of discovering, when the next appointment comes, whether it was a hello or a goodbye.

items.title: Lipari off-season: history, tradition and political exiles on an island of memories
items.summary: A journey to the queen of the Aeolian Islands, where time stands still and getting there depends on the whims of the gods
items.content:
There is no room for ambiguity on the departure boards at Milazzo. Just one word: “Cancelled.” In winter — and not only then — a journey to the Aeolian Islands aboard a high-speed ferry doesn't begin when you buy your ticket. It begins when the sea decides to let you cross.

Sometimes it's the sirocco, whipping up the waves. At other times, it's the mistral, sweeping into the harbour. And suddenly, time takes on a different meaning. It is no longer measured by a quartz clock. “Early” and “late” become one and the same. Because everything depends on the weather. Or rather, on Aeolus, the god of the winds.

Whether you can get to Messina for a medical appointment. Whether you can reach Lipari at all. There is an unwritten rule here: live according to nature's rhythms and accept that not everything is within your control. A kind of resignation that turns uncertainty into the very first stage of the journey.

When the summer tide of tourists recedes, the island returns to its original pace. Weekends are the exception, when islanders who work in Sicily or further afield return home, along with a few visitors travelling back and forth on high-speed ferries.

Marina Corta, a bustling waterfront during the warmer months, becomes a quiet seaside haven again. Fishing boats are hauled ashore onto the quay, safely out of reach of the winter storms. The murmur of conversation is confined to the handful of bars still open in the historic centre, while overhead there is only the wind, the clouds and the cries of seagulls.

Climbing from Marina Corta towards the Castle on a rainy or windy day brings the island's long history into sharp focus. Within its walls stands the Basilica of San Bartolomeo, reached by a long staircase cutting through the fortifications, with its Norman cloister tucked away behind a side entrance.

There is also the Luigi Bernabò Brea Archaeological Museum, home to an extraordinary collection that visitors can explore in complete solitude during winter, among ancient Greek masks and amphorae recovered from shipwrecks deep beneath the sea.

The museum has a distinctly old-fashioned charm, with its wooden and glass display cases and no augmented reality or special effects. Its appeal lies in the story it tells: that of an ancient civilisation and of the peoples who inhabited the Aeolian Islands without ever truly possessing them.

Experiencing all this in peace feels like a rare privilege. That heritage lives on in local traditions, kept alive by folk groups such as the Cantori Popolari delle Isole Eolie.

But the Castle is also a place of political and civic memory. During the Fascist era, it became one of Italy's main centres of internal exile. Intellectuals and anti-Fascists including Carlo Rosselli, Emilio Lussu and Ferruccio Parri walked within these stone walls before their extraordinary escape by boat to France in 1929.

Looking out to sea from the battlements, imagining those nights of imprisonment and waiting, it becomes clear how Lipari was, for centuries, both a fortress and an open-air prison.

Inside the Castle, visitors can see the quarters where people banished from mainland Italy for refusing to submit to the ruling regime were housed.

But virtually the entire town of Lipari became a place of exile. Those sent to the island often had to find accommodation in rented or requisitioned houses and large communal rooms scattered throughout the town.

Plaques in the narrow streets commemorate those forced into exile on the island, including Curzio Malaparte and Edda Ciano, who was sent there after the fall of the Fascist regime.

Each location is marked by one of 50 ceramic tiles identifying former places of confinement. A web app, developed partly with funding from NextGenerationEU, allows visitors to discover them one by one and learn the stories of those who were forced to live there.

Beyond the town, Lipari in the off-season reveals its volcanic soul and a past shaped by more than the sea.

At Porticello, the former pumice quarries offer a striking glimpse of the Aeolian Islands' industrial heritage. Rusting structures and old piers stretch into the Tyrrhenian Sea, while a mountain of white “snow” meets the deep blue water.

Pumice has been extracted on Lipari for centuries. But it was only in the 20th century, with the introduction of a structured industrial plan, that quarrying became a significant part of the island's economy.

Lipari pumice, prized for its remarkable whiteness and physical properties, has also been used in the clothing industry, particularly to give jeans a worn appearance.

Although the industry provided an important source of income for generations of islanders, inadequate safety measures and exposure to silica caused respiratory illnesses, including silicosis, among many workers over the decades.

Towards Quattropani, the land still bears signs of its volcanic past. The trail through the Kaolin Quarries winds between rocks shimmering with golden and violet hues before reaching the vapours rising from sulphurous fumaroles.

Not far away, the tholos-shaped dome of the ancient Terme di San Calogero bears witness to a tradition of thermal bathing dating all the way back to the Mycenaean period.

The baths have long been closed to the public, but the site remains an essential stop for understanding the profound relationship between people and the geology of this remarkable landscape.

Away from the coast, several wineries produce Malvasia. Not simply a sweet dessert wine, but also a dry, complex wine that captures the aromas of volcanic soil and the salty sea air. Among them is Tenuta di Castellaro, perched on a hill that drops almost sheer towards the sea, with views across to Salina. The estate, which produces some of the island's finest Malvasia, also boasts a striking underground cellar where barrels are stored and tastings featuring local produce are held.

It’s only a short step from wine to food. In winter, many local dishes feature pulses and salt-preserved capers. And, of course, there is excellent fresh local fish.

Then there are traditional Christmas sweets, although they can actually be found throughout the year, such as nacatole: filled biscuits intricately decorated to resemble crocheted lace.

For a complete introduction to Aeolian flavours, just below the Castle stands the historic and celebrated Filippino restaurant, an ideal place to discover traditional island cuisine with a contemporary twist.

From Lipari, weather permitting, it is easy to reach its neighbouring islands. One of the experiences recommended by Lonely Planet in its Best in Travel 2027 is to explore them by sailing boat.

Vulcano, with its natural sulphurous thermal baths; Salina, with its elegance and cliffs plunging into the sea; Stromboli, with its slightly precarious air.

Each is different, yet all share extraordinary beauty and the slow rhythm of island life, when the tourist season ends and another way of living begins.

The journey home will once again involve negotiating with the sea. But after seeing Lipari when the spotlight fades, even waiting for a ferry that never arrives ceases to be a problem.

items.title: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
items.summary: The vice-president's blunt assessment of Republican election defeat marked one of the sharpest breaks with a sitting president in recent memory.
items.content:
Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.

In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election .

"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."

In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate .

Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington. While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.

But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.

Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.

It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.

Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.

BOWEN: Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad

ZURCHER: Midterm carnage weakens Trump but he still wields power for now

'A DISASTER': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat

It was an early sign that Trump - who has prized loyalty from his advisers - may give Vance a wide berth should he choose to launch a presidential campaign.

"I know how he feels about it. I think it was -- I think it was fine," Trump told reporters when asked about Vance's post blaming the war. "I knew that when I went in, and we stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon."

Vance's statement seemed like "a way of separating himself from Trump," said Daniel Byman, a foreign policy expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

Drawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.

That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.

Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.

Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan: "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."

The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.

Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.

It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.

Trump, for his part, could change his mind and make clear he'll brook no dissent from Vance or anyone else.

The president has been circumspect about who he'd support to succeed him as the 2028 Republican presidential nominee. Trump has praised Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on several occasions, but hasn't said when - or if – he'd make an endorsement.

The president appears to relish the guessing game of who he'd back to carry on his political movement, even in the past floating the idea that he'd continue to a third term (which is barred by the US Constitution).

Vance's midterms missive might not be that significant in the end. Or it could have been the starting gun for the 2028 race and the battle for the post-Trump Republican Party.

items.title: Il deposito (definitivo) per scorie nucleari
items.summary: Il deposito (definitivo) per scorie nucleari
items.content:
Onkalo è la risposta finlandese alla questione più spinosa del nucleare, cioè cosa fare delle scorie. Con l'energia atomica di nuovo in espansione, anche per la ricerca di fonti a basse emissioni, servono risposte migliori. Sul fatto che la soluzione migliore sia seppellirle c'è ampio consenso, ma il problema è il tempo.
Impianti come questo, spiega Allison Macfarlane (Università della British Columbia, già presidente della Commissione di regolamentazione nucleare statunitense), devono restare intatti per almeno 100.000 anni, forse un milione: scale temporali geologiche.
La Grande Piramide ha circa 4.500 anni, mentre alcuni depositi dovranno contenere i rifiuti per un periodo oltre 20 volte più lungo, durante il quale potrebbero sorgere e tramontare civiltà e avanzare e ritirarsi le calotte glaciali.. Il problema delle scorie
Gran parte dei rifiuti nucleari presenta una bassa radioattività e si gestisce con relativa facilità. La vera sfida riguarda il combustibile esaurito e i materiali di schermatura del nocciolo: elementi come lo iodio-129, infatti, hanno un'emivita di quasi 16 milioni di anni.
Nel corso del tempo si è persino ipotizzato di spedire queste scorie nello Spazio, ma l'esperta Allison Macfarlane boccia l'idea ricordando il disastro dello shuttle Challenger: l'eventuale esplosione di un vettore disperderebbe materiale altamente cancerogeno nell'atmosfera. L'unica alternativa concreta rimane quella tradizionale: seppellirle a grandi profondità, un'operazione però tutt'altro che semplice.. Il precedente fallito: Asse II
Dal 1967 la Germania Ovest stoccò oltre 125.000 fusti di rifiuti a bassa e media attività nell'ex miniera di sale di Asse II. Il salgemma sembrava ideale perché impermeabile e capace di richiudere da sé le crepe. Nel 1988 si scoprì invece che vi penetrava acqua salata. Secondo un rapporto del 2011 dell'International Panel on Fissile Materials, i minatori avevano scavato troppo vicino al bordo dei depositi di sale e non avevano riempito a sufficienza le caverne, indebolendo la struttura e fratturando il sale più in fretta di quanto potesse sigillarsi.
Il rischio di crolli era stato segnalato già nel 1979, ma l'avvertimento fu ignorato. L'opinione pubblica lo seppe solo nel 2008 e oggi la Germania deve recuperare circa 47.000 metri cubi di scorie.. L'ipotesi del recupero
Un'alternativa allo stoccaggio definitivo parte dal presupposto che una sepoltura perenne potrebbe non essere necessaria: circa il 97% del combustibile esaurito è infatti riciclabile e la tecnologia futura potrebbe offrire opzioni più avanzate. Su questo principio si basa il progetto francese Cigéo (previsto per gli anni 2050 all'interno di argille impermeabili) dotato di una funicolare pensata per riportare le scorie in superficie in caso di necessità. Come rileva Allison Macfarlane, in Francia l'opinione pubblica vuole la certezza di poter intervenire qualora qualcosa andasse storto.. Tramandare la memoria
Resta poi il nodo della memoria: evitare che le civiltà future perforino il terreno per errore, ignare del pericolo sottostante. Negli Stati Uniti, per il Waste Isolation Pilot Plant del Nuovo Messico, si era pensato a monumenti respingenti, ipotesi poi scartata poiché le rovine misteriose finiscono spesso per attirare curiosi e cercatori di tesori. Macfarlane dubita che sia possibile concepire un cartello di pericolo comprensibile a distanza di millenni.
Per questo la Francia sta sperimentando dischi di zaffiro da 20 centimetri capaci di conservare fino a 40.000 pagine microscopiche resistenti a graffi, calore e sostanze chimiche. La Svezia punta invece su un documento digitale di 42 pagine costantemente tradotto e aggiornato per il sito di Forsmark, affidandosi anche alla trasmissione culturale: radicare queste informazioni nell'istruzione potrebbe rivelarsi più duraturo di qualsiasi supporto fisico, esattamente come le tradizioni orali degli aborigeni australiani hanno tramandato intatta la memoria dell'innalzamento dei mari avvenuto 7.000 anni fa.. L'approccio finlandese
La Finlandia ha scelto di non avvertire nessuno. Decenni fa i ricercatori cercarono un sottosuolo così povero di risorse (come il petrolio) da non attirare mai scavi, così che il deposito possa essere sigillato e dimenticato. Lo trovarono a Olkiluoto, nel sud-ovest del paese, dove dal 2004 si lavora a Onkalo. «Man mano che ci si addentra, l'ambiente si fa più silenzioso e la roccia più presente», racconta Petteri Vuorio, direttore dello sviluppo dell'impianto. La roccia è soprattutto gneiss, densissimo e impermeabile, mappato con cura per evitare fratture; i tunnel corrono solo nelle zone integre. A questo si aggiunge il sistema multibarriera KBS-3, sviluppato dalla svedese SKB. Il combustibile esaurito finisce in un contenitore di ghisa, sigillato in un recipiente di rame con pareti spesse 5 centimetri, il metallo che negli studi resta pressoché inalterato in ambienti radioattivi e ad alta pressione. Il contenitore è calato in un foro nella roccia e circondato da bentonite compattata. Questa argilla si gonfia a contatto con l'acqua, formando una barriera quasi impermeabile e ammortizza eventuali movimenti della roccia.. Come spiega la geologa Clare Bond dell'Università di Aberdeen, la barriera artificiale dovrebbe farcela da sola. Nell'ottobre 2026 il governo finlandese ha concesso la licenza operativa e nei prossimi mesi arriveranno i primi carichi. Una volta pieno, tutto sarà riempito di bentonite e sigillato: l'impianto scomparirà nella roccia. Il sito era sotto una spessa calotta glaciale appena 20.000 anni fa e potrebbe tornarci; il sollevamento della crosta quando il ghiaccio si ritira può causare fratture, ma questi scenari sono stati ampiamente ridimensionati.. E gli altri?
Onkalo non sarà l'ultimo. A Forsmark, in Svezia, i lavori sono iniziati con lo stesso sistema rame-bentonite-roccia, con operatività prevista negli anni 2030. Il Canada ha progetti simili, ancora lontani. Il Regno Unito, che possiede la maggiore scorta mondiale di plutonio di grado reattore, è ancora alla scelta del sito: due candidati in formazioni argillose nel nord-ovest dell'Inghilterra, vicino a Sellafield, con un contenimento multistrato simile a quello finlandese..

items.title: Australia's oldest department store David Jones folds after 188 years
items.summary: The brand's 38 physical stores and online site will continue to operate while receivers review its operations.
items.content:
David Jones, Australia's oldest department store chain, has gone into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk.

It comes after years of financial struggles for the 188-year-old retailer - known locally as DJs - as customers desert traditional shops for online shopping.

David Jones's physical and online stores will continue to operate while receivers FTI Consulting review the company, said voluntary administrators McGrathNicol.

"David Jones is an iconic company and so many Australians have stories and memories of visiting DJ's stores," said its CEO Erica Berthold, adding the brand has a "well-developed plan" to "reset the business for the future".

Berthold thanked "customers, our team members and our partners for their continued support of David Jones through this period".

David Jones employs about 6,000 staff and has 38 physical stores, with 17 of those in Westfield shopping centres.

Hours before the board voted to go into administration, Scentre - which owns Westfield - said the retailer had not paid its rent for October and was "therefore in breach" of its tenancy agreement.

"We understand the current retail trading environment, rising costs, a significant and outdated retail footprint, and supply chain challenges have led to this point," said Christopher Hill from receivers FTI Consulting.

By appointing administrators and receivers, David Jones will get "breathing space" and a chance to restructure the business, Hill said.

For many Australians, David Jones - and its trademark black-and-white houndstooth design - represented luxury.

But its collapse signalled the "death knell" for the department store format, said Jana Bowden, who teaches marketing at Macquarie University's Business School.

"It was once the epitome of glamour shopping in Australia - the Aussie version of Harrods," she said, "a place you would go to see and be a part of the glitz and glamour, where you could marvel at all the premium luxury labels, and feel like you'd made it."

Visiting the flagship city stores in Sydney and Melbourne was also a ritual for many Australian families, especially to see the festive Christmas window displays.

"People would travel from hours away from the city just to see those windows and experience the magic," Bowden said, but in recent years, the brand had lost its shine.

"The city stores have retained their upper end airs and graces, but the suburban stores leave a lot to be desired – they're mundane, they lack excitement and there's definitely no glitz," she said.

During Queen Elizabeth II's first visit to Sydney in 1954, the then-27-year-old monarch attended a banquet dinner on the seventh floor of the Elizabeth St store, according to the Sydney Morning Herald.

items.title: Would you take a test to see if your life will be cut short? I did - and it changed me
items.summary: Laura Sides faced a dilemma of whether to find out if she would inherit her father's condition.
items.content:
If you could find out if you had a gene that would cut your life short, would you?

This is the dilemma Laura Sides faced when she was offered a test for the rare form of early onset dementia that her dad was diagnosed with in his 40s.

Laura spoke to Dr Sian Williams, host of BBC Radio 4's Life Changing podcast, about her decision to take the test and how it has shaped the rest of her life.

Growing up, Laura says she always felt close to her dad as they had a "similar nature". He was a GP and "the most amazing doting father," she says. When his Alzheimer's symptoms became more severe, Laura dropped out of university to care for him.

"We did have a really lovely time," she says, remembering trips to a lighthouse and collecting coasters. " I'd run him baths and just play music and pour jugs of hot water over his head and he loved it."

It was at a hospital appointment with her dad when a doctor told Laura she had a 50/50 chance of developing the same type of early onset Alzheimer's known as the "London variant".

"All I could think was, that's a toss of a coin," she says. "I was still so involved with what was going on with him [her dad]. I just pushed it really, really deep down."

Laura's dad died in 2009, just a year after her mum had died.

"All of a sudden I got such an overwhelming urge to leave," she says. So she booked a solo around-the-world trip, eventually settling in Melbourne, Australia.

It was there that thoughts of inheriting her dad's condition "started creeping in" and she went to see a specialist in 2013.

He told her a test could determine with 99.999% certainty if she would inherit early onset dementia. If she had the gene, her expected age of decline would be 46 to 48, he said.

"I just thought, I'm not there yet. I don't want to do that."

As Laura entered her 30s she found herself thinking about the test more and more and decided she wanted to know. But first, she had to undergo six months of genetic counselling.

"There's not many realms in life where you find out your fate and it can be very difficult information to process," she says.

After a six-week wait for the test results to come through, the day finally arrived. Laura says she felt "extremely nervous".

She had booked a table for lunch with a friend afterwards - but went into the appointment alone.

"I said, 'Let's cut straight to it.' They said, 'We're really sorry, it's not good news, and you have inherited the gene.'"

She remembers "almost a white blurry noise of just sitting there".

"I came out of that room and my friend burst into hysterical tears." But Laura didn't react. "We went for our lunch and it was lovely. I don't know if it'd sunk in."

The reality hit later. "I was angry. I felt it was so unjust. I was just too confused at how I was meant to live now. How do you live with that knowledge?"

Laura began to feel a pull back home to the UK, especially as her sister was pregnant. "It doesn't make sense... to live on the other side of the world when she's going to have a baby."

However, her around-the-world travels continued as she took part in medical trials before and after her diagnosis.

"It felt like such a positive to be involved in something out of such a negative situation."

Laura is now 43 - three years away from the age doctors predicted she will begin to notice symptoms.

"I keep waiting for something to sort of hit home. I guess one day I'll start declining but that doesn't keep me up at night."

She is "grateful and so lucky for the people in her life". But meeting anyone new is hard.

"Do I tell them? Do I not tell them? At what point do I tell them?

"I have been shown I can be loved despite this. It fills my heart with reassurance and joy".

Laura says she had always "naively assumed" she would be a mother.

"[Its] one of the very few things that I never questioned that I'd be good at and I wanted to do. That's hard... but it doesn't make sense to do it. It wouldn't be fair."

For Laura, life is now about tapping in to things that "make her happy".

"It's not about huge aspirations. It's not like I want to see the Grand Canyon... I want to have time now around the people that I adore and make me feel safe.

"I love nature. I love being outside. I'm obsessed with being submerged in water. It sounds so corny, but...I believe it really is actually the little things are the big things.

"I hope I just have a wonderful few years in this world... drinking champagne and eating oysters - two of my favourite things."

If you or someone you know has been affected by dementia, you can access support from the BBC Action Line.

items.title: Why a US-funded vaccine trial on babies was cancelled in Guinea-Bissau
items.summary: The trial was condemned as "unethical" and "neocolonial" because half of the babies would not be given the vaccine.
items.content:
A proposed trial of a hepatitis B vaccine on newborn babies in Guinea-Bissau has been cancelled following accusations that the trial was "unethical" and "neocolonial".

The trial was funded by the US, under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has a long record of expressing scepticism about vaccines.

Police have seized a batch of vaccines from the research centre at the heart of the controversy.

The proposed trial drew international criticism because it planned to withhold a vaccine recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) from half of the participating newborns.

Some public health experts argued that the proposed trial raised broader questions about whether vulnerable populations in African countries were being asked to take risks that researchers would not accept in wealthier countries.

The BBC has asked the US department of health and human services for comment.

The study was planned at the Bandim Health Project, a research centre that has operated in Guinea-Bissau since 1978.

It was designed to involve 14,000 newborns, with half receiving a hepatitis B vaccine shortly after birth and the other half not being given the shot .

Bandim said the trial aimed to investigate whether the hepatitis B vaccine given at birth has broader health effects beyond preventing infection.

Previous studies in The Gambia and Guinea-Bissau have raised questions about a possible link to increased mortality.

Researchers argued that because Guinea-Bissau does not currently offer routine hepatitis B vaccinations at birth, despite WHO recommendations, they have a unique opportunity to study its effects before such vaccines are introduced in 2028.

But critics questioned the ethics of withholding the vaccine from some babies, particularly in one of the world's poorest countries, where the infection is widespread.

The Trump administration funded the proposed study, with the CDC awarding the University of Southern Denmark (SDU) $1.6m (£1.2m) in December 2025 .

Walter Kazadi Mulombo, the WHO representative in Guinea-Bissau, told the BBC they became concerned after receiving questions about the study and finding no publicly available protocol.

He said the main ethical concern was that the trial would withhold an intervention already proven to protect newborns against hepatitis B.

"The vaccine has been used for more than 30 years in more than 115 countries," he said. "A study that will withhold that intervention from other newborns is unethical."

He warned that babies could be exposed to the virus during childbirth if their mothers were infected, as well as later in life.

Nearly a fifth of the population of Guinea-Bissau are infected with hepatitis B, a viral infection that affects the liver.

Those infected during infancy are particularly likely to develop chronic infections, which kill up to 25% of people, mostly through liver failure or liver cancer, according to data published in 2020.

The WHO is working with the government to bring forward the birth-dose vaccine.

"The country had been expected to add it to its routine immunisation schedule in 2028, but officials are considering introducing it in the first quarter of next year," Mulombo said.

Guinea-Bissau currently vaccinates children against hepatitis B at six weeks, which means it is less effective.

Guinea-Bissau's government prohibited hepatitis B vaccine trials involving children in January. At the time, it requested a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study.

Health Minister Quinhin Nantote said in October that the suspension remained in force and had not been overturned by the Council of Ministers after reports emerged claiming that the trial would be taking place after all.

"We were surprised to learn from media reports that the study might proceed," Nantote said. "We are outraged because even I, as the minister responsible for this sector, was not informed."

The dispute intensified after the SDU said a revised study protocol had received ethical approval "from the relevant authorities in Guinea-Bissau", which Nantote denied.

Dr Gavin Yamey, a professor of global health and public policy at Duke University in the US, criticised the proposal.

"The proposed trial reeks of neocolonialism," he told the BBC, questioning why the research was not being conducted in Denmark.

His criticism centred on the decision to withhold a recommended vaccine from some newborns in a country where hepatitis B is widespread.

SDU dean Jakob Grauslund said the trial had never started, no babies had been enrolled and no vaccinations administered as part of the research.

The SDU said it had received a separate, positive assessment from the university's own research ethics committee.

Grauslund said the university had sought an additional independent assessment, although Danish law did not require one.

He added that the relevant Danish statutory research ethics bodies were unable to undertake the review.

Following the approval from the SDU's ethics committee, Grauslund decided that the project could proceed.

He, however, stressed that this did not replace the separate authorisation required from Guinea-Bissau's authorities.

On 19 October, Guinea-Bissau's Judicial Police searched the Bandim Health Project's facilities in the capital, Bissau, and seized a batch of hepatitis B vaccines.

Police said the batch was intended for vaccinating children but did not disclose how many doses had been seized or the specific grounds for the investigation.

They stressed that the seizure did not, in itself, mean the vaccines were defective or unsafe.

The police have not explicitly said whether their investigation relates to the proposed trial, the importation of the vaccines or other circumstances surrounding the batch.

Grauslund said he could not comment on the seizure of the vaccines.

The proposed trial was funded by the US government at a time of significant changes to vaccine policy under President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Kennedy.

Under Kennedy's leadership, a US vaccine panel attempted to end a longstanding recommendation that all newborns receive a hepatitis B vaccine at birth, but a federal judge later blocked this, along with other changes to vaccine policy made by the Trump administration.

Critics have questioned whether the research could help support that policy shift, although the study's stated aim was to investigate potential effects of the vaccine beyond preventing infection.

Kennedy has praised the Danish researchers as "the deities of vaccine research", and cited earlier findings from their work in support of concerns about vaccine safety. A subsequent study by some of the same researchers, however, found no evidence of the previously reported effect.

There is no evidence that the proposed trial was designed to justify a change in US policy.
